verses.translation_literal: And it was in the days of Amraphel, king of Shinar, Arioch, king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and Tidal, king of Goyim,
verses.translation_dramatic: It was in the days of four crowns: Amraphel, king of Shinar; Arioch, king of Ellasar; Chedorlaomer, king of Elam; and Tidal, king of Goyim.
verses.directors_commentary:
The chapter opens like a chronicle, not a story: four kings, four names, four far-off lands, and a sentence that hangs unfinished until verse 2 supplies the verb. Play it as a roll call read in a royal court; the audience should feel the sheer distance from the little tents of Abram. 'In the days of' is how ancient writers fix an event in history by naming the rulers of the day, as the Babylonian and Assyrian year-lists do. Shinar is Mesopotamia, the land of Babel; Elam lies east of the Tigris in what is now south-west Iran, and Chedorlaomer's name sounds Elamite, which would suit the king who turns out to be the senior partner.

The KJV stumbles on the last name: 'Tidal king of nations' treats goyim as a common noun, while the ASV and the rest keep 'Goiim' as a name. The Hebrew allows both. Rashi and Radak take it as a place settled by gathered peoples, Ibn Ezra offers the same or 'king of nations'. Tradition also loved to decode the list: Rashi, following Genesis Rabbah, makes Amraphel Nimrod, the one who had Abram thrown in the furnace; Ramban reads the four kings as the four world empires. These are traditional readings, not the plain sense.

philological_notes.note: Amraphel, king of Shinar. Rashi, citing Genesis Rabbah, identifies him with Nimrod, playing on 'amar pol' ('he said: fall!' into the fiery furnace). A midrashic pun, not an etymology.

Either the name of a place or people, 'Goyim', or the plain noun 'nations'. Rashi and Radak say a place so called because it was settled by people gathered from many nations; Onkelos translates it as 'peoples'.

verses.translation_literal: They made war with Bera, king of Sodom, and with Birsha, king of Gomorrah, Shinab, king of Admah, and Shemeber, king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, that is Zoar.
verses.translation_dramatic: And these four made war on the kings of the plain: Bera of Sodom, Birsha of Gomorrah, Shinab of Admah, Shemeber of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the sentence of verse 1 finally gets its verb: 'they made war'. The KJV's opening 'That these made war' inserts a 'that' the Hebrew does not have and so makes the whole thing read as a subordinate clause. The weight falls on the second list. Five little city-states of the Jordan plain, none of them named a great power, are set against the four empires of the east. Notice that the first four kings are named and the last is not; Bela, a small town with few people, gets no king's name (Ramban), and the narrator hurries to say it is Zoar, the name that will matter later.

The names of the plain-kings sound like a curse list, and the rabbis heard it so: Bera is 'in evil', Birsha 'in wickedness', Shinab 'hater of father' and Shemeber 'he put on a wing' (to fly in rebellion), in Rashi's reading; the Targum adds the same puns. Whether the biblical writer meant a deliberate distortion of real names is a question, but an ancient audience would hear ra' and resha' in the first two. The preposition 'et' here means 'with' in the sense of 'against', as in the English 'wage war with'.

philological_notes.note: Bera, king of Sodom. Sounds like ra', 'evil'; Rashi reads it as 'evil to heaven and evil to people'. Birsha (next) likewise echoes resha', 'wickedness'.
The king of Bela has no personal name; Ramban explains that Bela was a small city with few people and no renown abroad. The narrator adds that Bela is Zoar, the town Lot later asks for.

verses.translation_literal: All these joined together to the valley of Siddim; it is the Sea of Salt.
verses.translation_dramatic: All of them gathered at the Valley of Siddim, the valley that is now the Salt Sea.
verses.directors_commentary:
A quiet verse between two lists, and a narrator's aside. The armies converge on a single place, and the place is already gone: the writer says 'it is the Sea of Salt' in the present tense, as if pointing across the water at a vanished plain. Let the actors feel that the ground under their feet is doomed, without ever hinting that they know it.

Who are 'all these'? The Hebrew does not say, and the commentators split. Radak takes it as the four kings together with the five; Sforno, that Amraphel's side and the rest struck an agreement there. The KJV's 'were joined together' is passive and vague; the Hebrew verb is active, 'they joined forces', and the 'to' (el) is movement toward the valley, which Radak says is equivalent to 'in'. The Salt Sea is the Dead Sea; Rashi says the sea later flowed over the valley, so the name is the narrator's, not the kings'.

Measure: the Dead Sea surface lies more than 400 metres below sea level, the lowest dry land on earth, so a plain here is a hot, sunken basin.

philological_notes.note: 'They joined, allied' (Qal). Ibn Ezra notes it is in the simple (light) stem. The subject is only 'all these', so who joined whom is open: the five as a muster, or the four with the five.
Valley of Siddim. Rashi derives it from sadeh, 'fields', because it had many fields; Radak notes the Aramaic Targum renders 'the fields'.

verses.translation_literal: Twelve years they served Chedorlaomer, and [in the] thirteenth year they rebelled.
verses.translation_dramatic: Twelve years they bowed to Chedorlaomer. In the thirteenth, they rose against him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reason for the war, told in two beats of grammar: 'they served' ('avdu), 'they rebelled' (maradu), the same three-syllable shape, the same stress, the second snapping the first. Twelve long years of obedience, then one year of defiance. Play it as a slow burn.

The actors need the economics. In the ancient Near East a vassal 'served' by paying yearly tribute, in silver, grain, livestock, and goods, and by keeping the overlord's roads open; Radak says exactly this, that they were servants who carried a gift. Rebellion is nothing so noble as a freedom movement: it is simply to stop sending the gift (Radak). A great king would answer such default with an army, as the next verse shows. The KJV's 'in the thirteenth year' supplies a preposition the Hebrew lacks; the plain text says 'thirteen year they rebelled', and the singular 'year' after the number is ordinary Hebrew.

The subject of 'they served' is not named. Rashi supplies the five kings; Sforno ties the twelve years to the agreement they had reached in the valley.

philological_notes.note: 'They served', the normal verb for the subjection of a vassal to an overlord; Radak specifies service as bringing tribute.
'They rebelled'. Radak glosses it as rebelling and no longer bringing him a gift. The word answers 'avdu in sound and rhythm.

verses.translation_literal: And in the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer came, and the kings who [were] with him, and they struck the Rephaim in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzim in Ham, and the Emim in Shaveh Kiriathaim,
verses.translation_dramatic: In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer came, and the kings who stood with him. And they struck the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim at Ham, the Emim at Shaveh-kiriathaim,
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer to rebellion is a march. Chedorlaomer does not go straight for the rebels; he sweeps the long road down the east side of the Jordan first, breaking the peoples along it, so that when he turns on the plain no ally is left. Radak guesses these peoples were the plain-kings' friends, and Sforno that they fought for the five. Either way the audience should hear the roll of defeated names as a hammer tapping off the neighbours one by one, a distance of well over a thousand kilometres from Elam.

The verb is singular, 'Chedorlaomer came', and only then 'and the kings with him': he is the commander and the others are his allies (Rashi counts the three other kings). The KJV's 'smote the Rephaims... Zuzims... Emims' piles an English plural 's' on words already plural in Hebrew. These are old, frightening folk. Ibn Ezra hears in Rephaim the word for the dead or the weak and in Emim emah, 'terror'; Rashi says the Zuzim are the Zamzummim. Ashteroth Karnaim is 'Ashtaroth of the two horns', named, it seems, for a goddess and for the twin peaks (Radak says the place lies between two great mountains).

philological_notes.note: The Rephaim, tall ancient people of Bashan; the word elsewhere means the shades of the dead. Ibn Ezra says those who saw them lost heart and thought them dead; Radak calls them giants.
The Emim, 'the terrors'; Ibn Ezra explains the name as from emah, dread.
'Two horns': Radak says the place lies between two great mountains. The first element 'Ashteroth' is the plural of the name of the goddess Ashtoreth; I note that as my own reading.

verses.translation_literal: And the Horite in their hill-country, Seir, as far as El Paran, which [is] upon the wilderness.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the Horites in their hills of Seir, all the way to El-paran, where the wilderness begins.
verses.directors_commentary:
The march goes on south. No new verb: 'struck' from verse 5 carries over, and the sentence lengthens like the road. The Horites are the old people of the hill country of Seir, the rugged land south of the Dead Sea that Edom will later take over. 'Their hill-country' (har-ram) is the Hebrew's own detail, and the KJV's 'their mount Seir' is acceptable, while the BBE's 'driving them' invents a verb. Ibn Ezra and Radak argue over the grammar of the word, and Onkelos translates it as 'their mountains'.

El Paran is the knot. Onkelos has 'plain of Paran' and Rashi follows, saying 'el' is the name of such a plain. Ramban disagrees, saying it means a place of rams or oaks (cf. 'elon), a point he argues at length. I follow the plain reading as a name and leave the etymology open. The phrase 'upon the wilderness' means 'beside', as Rashi explains. This is the southern limit of the sweep: where the green hills give out to the open desert.

philological_notes.note: El Paran, 'at the edge of the wilderness'. Onkelos and Rashi read 'el' as a plain; Ramban argues for a place of rams or terebinths and compares 'Elon Mamre'.
'In their mountain', a form with a doubled middle consonant; Ibn Ezra reads it from the intensive stem, Radak from the noun har, which is the more natural reading.

verses.translation_literal: And they turned back and came to En Mishpat, it [is] Kadesh, and struck all the field of the Amalekite, and also the Amorite who was dwelling in Hazazon Tamar.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then they turned back and came to En-mishpat, the Spring of Judgment, which is Kadesh. And they struck all the country of the Amalekites, and the Amorites too, who lived in Hazazon-tamar.
verses.directors_commentary:
At the desert's edge the army wheels around and heads north, back toward the plain, with a stop at an oasis. En Mishpat means 'spring of judgment'. In a dry land a spring is where roads meet and quarrels are settled, so a place named for judgment suggests a court under the open sky, as Onkelos and Ramban's reading of the Aramaic suggest. Rashi, from the midrash, hears a hint of the future (Moses and Aaron judged at the waters of Meribah), and the narrator adds 'it is Kadesh' for readers who know it by the later name. The text does not say Kedorlaomer attacked the spring itself.

The verse carries an apparent anachronism: 'the Amalekite', though Amalek, Esau's grandson, was not yet born. Rashi says it is named for the future, Ramban offers an older Horite Amalek, and Radak says Moses simply used the name the land had when he wrote. The KJV's 'country' translates sadeh, 'field', meaning the open range of a people, as in 'the field of Edom' (Radak). 'Smote' is archaic for 'struck'. Hazazon Tamar, 'the pruning of palms', is En-gedi on the shore of the Dead Sea (Rashi, with 2 Chronicles 20:2); the army is now at the plain's doorstep.

philological_notes.note: 'Spring of judgment', explained as a gathering place for judgment (Onkelos), or, by midrash, for the later judgment of Moses and Aaron at Meribah. Ramban doubts the midrash and notes this Kadesh is the Kadesh of Paran.
'The field of the Amalekite'. A large plain with cities is called a field (Radak). The name is anachronistic if Amalek is Esau's grandson; Rashi, Ramban and Radak each resolve it differently.

verses.translation_literal: And the king of Sodom went out, and the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Admah, and the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, it [is] Zoar, and they arrayed with them battle in the valley of Siddim,
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the king of Sodom went out, and the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar. And in the Valley of Siddim they drew up their battle line against them.
verses.directors_commentary:
At last the five come out. The verb 'went out' is singular and each king gets his own 'and the king of', one after another: five kings, five separate gates opening. Let the pacing be slow and the repetition heavy, as five small armies take the field.

The verb 'arrayed' (ya'arkhu) is a military term for drawing up a line of battle, which the KJV flattens to 'joined battle'; the ASV's 'set the battle in array' is closer. Radak sees a sign of how the five regarded it: they thought themselves strong enough, perhaps with outside help, so they chose to fight rather than wait for a siege. The Hebrew preposition 'itam' is 'with them', and the sense is 'against'. The kings' names are not repeated this time, which makes them sound less like persons than offices: the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah. The Qere/Ketiv at Zeboiim, as in verse 2, changes only the spelling.

philological_notes.note: 'They arrayed, set in order' battle lines; a technical term for drawing up an army, softened by the KJV to 'joined battle'.

verses.translation_literal: With Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and Tidal, king of Goyim, and Amraphel, king of Shinar, and Arioch, king of Ellasar: four kings with the five.
verses.translation_dramatic: Against Chedorlaomer of Elam, Tidal of Goyim, Amraphel of Shinar, and Arioch of Ellasar: four kings against the five.
verses.directors_commentary:
The narrator pauses to count: four kings, five kings. A reader's first reaction is that five should beat four, and the verse exists to tell us they did not. Rashi's point is that the four were mighty, and yet Abram would still go after them, which the story is about to show. Radak adds that the four were only those named, with no hidden allies, and that the victory was granted so that Abram's name would be made great.

The order of the four has changed from verse 1. There Amraphel came first and Chedorlaomer third; here Chedorlaomer leads, as the true commander, with Amraphel moved to the third place. The Hebrew 'et' is the small word that confuses the English: 'with' in KJV and Webster can mean either allied with or against, and the ASV and BBE choose 'against'. Ibn Ezra simply glosses it as 'im'. The final phrase puts the numbers side by side, 'four kings with the five', with no verb; read it flat, like a scoreboard.

philological_notes.note: Here the preposition 'with', in the sense 'against' in a battle context (compare 14:2). Not the object marker. Ibn Ezra glosses it 'im'.

verses.translation_literal: And the valley of Siddim [was] pits, pits of bitumen, and the king of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and fell there, and those left fled to the hill.
verses.translation_dramatic: Now the Valley of Siddim was pit upon pit of bitumen. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah broke and ran, and fell there; and those who were left fled to the hills.
verses.directors_commentary:
The battle itself takes no time at all; the narrator gives instead the ground. The valley is 'pits, pits of bitumen', the word repeated to make a honeycomb of holes, as the Targum's 'pit after pit' also does. Bitumen is natural asphalt, black tar that seeps up around the Dead Sea; the Greeks later called the sea Asphaltites. People of the Near East dug it for mortar and for waterproofing, and Rashi says they quarried the clay from these pits for building. It is a trap of sticky ground, and soldiers fleeing in panic would run straight into it.

The KJV's 'slimepits' is a seventeenth-century word for bitumen and misleads: 'slime' sounds like mud, but this is tar. 'Fell there' is ambiguous. It may mean the kings dropped into the pits (so Ibn Ezra and Radak) or that they fell in battle (so the BBE, 'came to their end'). Tradition tells a story of the king of Sodom miraculously escaping the pit (Rashi), and Ramban doubts it. 'Hereh' is an old directional ending, 'toward the hill', which Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take pains to explain. Sforno says the survivors who fled were the three other kings.

philological_notes.note: 'Pits of bitumen'. The noun for 'pit' is repeated (be'erot be'erot) to say the valley was riddled with them; Rashi says clay was dug there for building mortar; Ramban takes them as pits of mire, like the pit that held Jeremiah.
'They fell there', either into the pits or in battle. Ibn Ezra reads it as falling in their wish to escape; Radak that they sank in the mire and did not die.
'Toward the hill-country', with the old directional ending -ah, equal to 'to the hill' (Rashi, Radak); Ibn Ezra calls it an unusual word.

verses.translation_literal: And they took all the property of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their food, and they went.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the victors took everything: all the wealth of Sodom and Gomorrah, every scrap of their food. Then they went.
verses.directors_commentary:
The cities lie open and the conquerors help themselves. Everything about the sentence is plain and flat: 'they took', 'they took', 'they went', three verbs and no emotion. Play it cold. This is how ancient warfare pays for itself: the winners strip the stores, livestock and movable wealth, and march home. Radak explains that the word for property, rekhush, covers all movable goods including herds. It comes from a root meaning 'to acquire', and it is the same word the narrator used for Abram's and Lot's own holdings in 13:6, so the audience will already be thinking of Lot.

The KJV's 'victuals' is archaic for 'food', and its 'went their way' adds 'their way' that is not in the Hebrew, which says only 'and they went'. Food is named last and with emphasis, 'and all their food': an army that has marched over a thousand kilometres needs it, and a city without its stores cannot hold out.

philological_notes.note: 'Property, goods acquired'; Radak says it includes movable goods and livestock. The same word describes Abram's and Lot's holdings in the chapters before.

verses.translation_literal: And they took Lot and his possessions, son of the brother of Abram, and they went; and he [was] dwelling in Sodom.
verses.translation_dramatic: And among all that they carried off, they took a man. Lot. The brother's son of Abram. They took him with his goods and they went, and the road swallowed them. He had been living in Sodom. That was all it took.
verses.directors_commentary: After eleven verses of kings and wars, Abram's name suddenly slips in, and it comes as a relation, not as a player: "son of the brother of Abram." Hold that beat. The story turns on a family tie, and the camera has just found the man who cares about it. Lot is listed with his goods because in a raid, people and property are one haul: captives were labour or ransom. Sforno reads it so: they seized Lot because he was Abram's kin, knowing his wealth, and hoping Abram would redeem him for a great sum. The last clause, "and he was dwelling in Sodom," is a participle, a man settled in place, and the actor should let the irony land. Radak ties it to 13:12, where Lot pitched his tent "as far as Sodom"; he had since moved in. Rashi asks who caused this to happen to him and answers: his living in Sodom. The KJV smooths the order, moving "who dwelt in Sodom" up beside Lot's name and turning the Hebrew's final flat clause into an aside; the Hebrew ends on "Sodom" like a door closing. YLT's parenthesis is closer. The KJV also turns the participle into a past, "dwelt"; the Hebrew says he is, at this moment, a resident.

philological_notes.note: Literally "son of the brother of Abram". The narrator spells out the tie so that the reader knows why Abram will act; the next verse's "brother" (אָחִיו, v.14) then widens it to "kinsman".
"Property, movable goods"; the same word frames the whole rescue (vv.11, 16, 21), so Lot's recovery is counted among the goods.

verses.translation_literal: And he came, the fugitive, and he told to Abram the Hebrew, and he was dwelling at the great trees of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner, and they were masters of the covenant of Abram.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then one man came, a survivor, breathless from the wreck of the valley, and he laid it all before Abram the Hebrew, the wanderer from across the river, who was camped under the great trees of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol, brother of Aner. These were men bound to Abram by a covenant sworn.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene opens with one man and one fact: a survivor stumbles into camp. The word "fugitive" (palit) is the same word as "escaped" in the KJV, but it carries weight in a chapter about a battle in which the kings of the Dead Sea cities fell (v.10) and fled. This man is the only link between a lost war and the one man who might do something about it. Ibn Ezra reads palit as someone who escaped the Sodomites, citing Ezekiel 33:21.

The unique epithet "the Hebrew" is the first time the word ivri appears in the Bible. Rashi hears "from across the river" (ever), and Radak derives it from Eber, ancestor of Abram. Either way the narrator is naming Abram from outside, the way foreigners and a messenger would, not the way Israel names itself. Sforno adds that the fugitive does not know that Abram and Lot are kin; he knows only that Abram holds Eber's beliefs.

The KJV is mostly accurate but twice misleading. "The plain of Mamre" is an old mistranslation of elonei, "the great trees, terebinths or oaks"; ASV corrects it. And "confederate" for baalei berit softens a vivid phrase: they are literally "masters of covenant", men who owned a treaty with Abram. In the ancient world that is an alliance with obligations, which is why Mamre, Eshcol and Aner will march with him and expect a share in v.24. Radak explains that Abram lived with these brothers, and they helped him.

philological_notes.note: 'The Hebrew', first occurrence. Traditionally 'from across (ever) the river' or 'descendant of Eber'; used in the Bible mainly by outsiders about Israelites. Whether it also relates to a social class of the second millennium is debated and I do not decide it here.
Literally 'masters of a covenant'; idiom for allies bound by treaty. Rashi: those who made a covenant with him.

verses.translation_literal: And Abram heard that his kinsman had been taken captive, and he drew out his trained men, those born of his house, eighteen and three hundred, and pursued as far as Dan.
verses.translation_dramatic: Abram heard. Only that: a kinsman taken, bound, gone. And he did not send word, and he did not wait. He opened his own household and drew them out like blades from a sheath: three hundred and eighteen, trained, born under his roof. And he ran after them. North. North, to Dan.
verses.directors_commentary: Abram has no army; he has a household, and it is the household that goes to war. "Born of his house" means home-born retainers, not hired men or levies: loyalty here is family loyalty, which is why the number can be so exact and so small. The KJV's "armed his trained servants" fixes the verb וַיָּרֶק as "armed," which is Rashi's and Radak's sense (from the idiom "to empty out a sword"); the plain sense is "drew out," and the image is of men poured out of a vessel. The adjective "trained" (חֲנִיכָיו) occurs only here, from the root of dedication and training (cf. Prov 22:6). Ibn Ezra says Abram had drilled them in war many times; Radak says he trained them in the way of truth to serve the LORD. The KJV's "servants" misses that: these are drilled men, not domestics, and YLT's "trained domestics" half repairs it. Kinsman: "brother" (אָחִיו) again, stretching to a nephew; Radak compares 13:8, "we are men, brothers." The number 318 is exact in the Hebrew; the sages (Rashi, Radak) note that the letters of Eliezer's name add to 318 and that some said he alone went. Ibn Ezra rejects that reading as not what the text says. Distance: from Mamre by Hebron to Dan is well over a hundred miles, days of hard marching for a column on foot.

philological_notes.note: From the root "empty": to empty out, draw out. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as arming ("empty the sword"); Radak distinguishes the causative (give weapons to them) from the simple sense. "Drew out" keeps the image and the debate.
A word found only here in the Bible, from the root "to dedicate, to train" (as in "train up a child," Prov 22:6). It names men who were schooled for a task.

Radak holds the name stands for what the place was later called: Moses wrote it when the place was not yet called Dan but Leshem, and the tribe of Dan, who captured it, named it for their ancestor. He adds that perhaps a place was already called Dan in those days. Judges 18:29 records the later renaming of Laish.

verses.translation_literal: And he divided himself against them [by] night, he and his servants, and struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which [is] from the left of Damascus.
verses.translation_dramatic: Night came down, and Abram split the dark. He and his men, divided, closed on them from more than one side, and struck, and the camp broke. They ran. He hounded them on, mile after mile, as far as Hobah, on the left hand of Damascus, where the road falls away to the north.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a night raid, and the staging is the point: a small force cannot meet four kings in daylight, so it divides and strikes in the dark. The Hebrew "divided himself" is a reflexive, with the odd word order "against them night, he and his servants." Rashi reads the plain sense as the usual practice of pursuers, who spread out after fugitives scattering in all directions; Ramban gives the same picture, with the force split in two or three parts once darkness hid which road the enemy took. Sforno sees a stratagem: the enemy would think the whole countryside had risen, and the dark hid how few they were. Radak hears the night itself as divided, with the kings secure until midnight and then in flight. Take your pick, but play the chaos. Hobah "which is on the left of Damascus" gives a direction by the ancient habit of facing east: left is north. The KJV's "on the left hand" keeps the Hebrew literally and is correct, but a modern reader may not see that it means north; BBE has "north side". Ramban notes the great distance from Hebron to Damascus and suggests either many days of pursuit or a miracle. Rashi finds no place named Hobah and takes the name as a pointed rename for Dan, whose idolatry was to come.

philological_notes.note: A reflexive form of "to divide." The text says he "divided himself" with his servants; Rashi and Ramban read it as splitting the force, Radak as the night being divided.
Literally "from the left." In Hebrew the points of the compass are given from a viewer facing east, so "left" is north: Hobah lies north of Damascus.

verses.translation_literal: And he brought back all the property, and also Lot his brother and his property he brought back, and also the women and the people.
verses.translation_dramatic: And it was all there to be brought home: every scrap of the plunder, and Lot, his own kin, and Lot's goods with him. He brought back the women too, and the people, every one.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a ledger, and its repetition is the point. The verb "brought back" (hashiv, from shuv) occurs twice and its root a third time in v.17 ("his return"): Abram turns everything around. The Hebrew is stubbornly even: "all the property" first, then "Lot ... and his property", then "the women and the people", a list in which Lot is neither first nor last. The KJV flattens the double verb into "brought back ... brought again", which is correct, and adds "his brother Lot", also correct (see v.14).

What the KJV hides is that rekhush, "property", is a collective noun for movable wealth: flocks, tents, silver. It becomes important in v.21, when the king of Sodom divides persons from property. Radak points out that the people came back alive: none had been killed. Sforno says the women belong to Lot's household, while "the people" are the captives from Sodom, those the king of Sodom asks for in v.21. In the ancient Near East victors owned what they took; Abram's right to this booty is clear, which is why his refusal in v.22-24 is the choice of a free man, not a legal necessity.

philological_notes.note: Collective 'movable property, goods, plunder', frequently the spoil of war or the wealth of a nomad. The same word returns in v.21.

verses.translation_literal: And the king of Sodom went out to meet him, after his returning from striking Kedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, to the valley of Shaveh, that is the valley of the king.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the king of Sodom came out to meet him, now that the stroke was struck and Abram was turning homeward, with Kedorlaomer and the kings beside him broken. They met in the valley of Shaveh, the level ground they called the King's Valley.
verses.directors_commentary:
The king of Sodom, who fled the battle in v.10, now walks out to meet the man who did what he could not. The scene is staged as a state encounter: a king goes out "to meet" a victorious commander, the standard form for welcoming a returning army (cf. 1 Sam 18:6). Notice what the narrator does: the sentence is held in suspense. The king comes out, then we get the long reminder of the victory, then the place name, and only in v.21 does he speak. Between lies Melchizedek (v.18-20), as Rashbam observes.

The KJV "slaughter" for hakkot is stronger than the Hebrew "striking"; and "dale" for emek is an archaism for valley. Shaveh means "level, even" (Rashi, Radak): flat ground, free of trees and obstacles, where the king's riders trained their horses, in Radak's account. The identification of the King's Valley is unknown; in 2 Sam 18:18 Absalom builds his pillar there. The Aramaic Targum calls it beit risa, a racecourse.

The text names Kedorlaomer first, as the head of the coalition, "and the kings with him": the entire alliance is struck, not one army.

philological_notes.note: 'Valley of Shaveh': shaveh is 'level, even', so a plain flat valley. Rashi and Radak, following Onkelos, take it as open ground cleared of trees and stones.

verses.translation_literal: And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine; and he [was] priest of God Most High.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then, into the dust and the noise of men coming home, a new figure steps out of the day. Melchizedek, king of Salem. He comes carrying bread, and wine. He is a priest, a priest of God Most High.
verses.directors_commentary: The story stops its stride here. The king of Sodom has gone out (v.17) and we expect him to speak; instead the narrator interrupts with a second king, who brings food. Rashbam notices the interruption and reads it as a hint about who fed Abram's men. Bread and wine are the plain fare for tired soldiers coming from war: Radak and Sforno both say it was for the weary, and Rashi adds that this is what is done for those worn out by fighting. Salem is Jerusalem, as Ibn Ezra, Ramban and Radak all say, citing Psalm 76:3 ("in Salem his booth"). The name "Melchizedek" is read as "my king is righteousness," or "Zedek is my king"; the Hebrew allows both, and Ibn Ezra explains it as a king of a place of righteousness. Radak links it to the later king "Adoni-zedek" (Josh 10:1), as Ramban does. Audit the KJV: it says "the priest of the most high God." The Hebrew has no article: "a priest of El Elyon." The KJV also reverses the word order, from "God Most High" to "most high God," which makes "most high" read as ordinary description rather than a title. BBE goes further and merges the verse with the next, making the priest himself the one who "took" the bread. Who is the god? The text names him "El Elyon" and does not say more here. Radak says Melchizedek served the Most High alone, "not the stars and constellations," as Abram did. Ramban says that since the nations have priests who serve the angels called "gods," the Holy One is called "El Elyon", the one above all; he adds that Melchizedek does not use the divine name YHWH, but Abram does in v.22 ("YHWH, El Elyon"), which joins the two names. Some modern scholars compare El Elyon with a high god attested in other ancient Near Eastern sources; that is a modern comparison, not something this text says, and the traditional readers above take it differently.

philological_notes.note: "Bread and wine": food and drink for men coming back from battle, in the commentators' reading, not a rite named by the text.

"A priest of God Most High." Ramban takes "El Elyon" as the Holy One's name in the mouths of the nations, "the strong one, high above all that are high"; Radak says the priesthood is to the Most High alone.

verses.translation_literal: And he blessed him and said: Blessed [be] Abram to God Most High, acquirer of heaven and earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he blessed him. Then he spoke, and the words rang out over the tired men: "Blessed be Abram, blessed by God Most High, who made heaven and earth his own."
verses.directors_commentary: He blesses first, then speaks: Sforno says the blessing proper came first, then the saying that Abram is already blessed by El Elyon, as was promised in 12:2 ("I will bless you"). The Hebrew word for blessed here is a passive participle, "Blessed [be] Abram", with the lamed ("to God Most High") marking whom the blessing belongs to. The KJV renders "of the most high God," where "of" is old English for "by": the sense is "blessed by God Most High," not "of" in the modern sense. The KJV's "possessor" for קֹנֵה is true to the Hebrew's "acquirer"; the word is the one Eve uses in 4:1, "I have acquired a man." The commentators debate whether it means "maker" or "owner": Rashi, Radak and Ramban lean towards "maker" because things that one makes become one's own; Ramban adds that the stronger sense is ownership. BBE has "maker" and YLT "possessing." The action is spoken, not performed: the Hebrew has the blessing and the saying, nothing else. This line is a claim in a world of regional gods: the one who owns heaven and earth is owner of the war that was just won.

philological_notes.note: "Acquirer, owner"; the root also gives "I have acquired a man" (Gen 4:1). Rashi reads it as "maker" (as in Psalm 134:3): by making, he acquired. Radak says it means "maker or provider"; Ramban says it can carry both senses, and adds that Onkelos renders it "whose are heaven and earth."

verses.translation_literal: And blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your adversaries into your hand. And he gave to him a tenth from everything.
verses.translation_dramatic: "And blessed be God Most High, who has handed your enemies over into your own hand." And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.
verses.directors_commentary:
The blessing turns from man to God: Abram is blessed, and the One who did it is blessed in return. The phrase "delivered into your hand" is the language of the battlefield and of the law: victory is a gift, not a conquest. The Hebrew verb magen is rare; Rashi and Radak explain it as "handed over", parallel to Hosea 11:8, and Ibn Ezra links it to Proverbs 4:9. The KJV "hath delivered" is right; the better-known sense "to shield" belongs to another noun (magen, a shield) and is not what the verb means here.

The last clause has no named subject: "and he gave him a tenth from everything". Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as Abram, giving a tenth of the plunder to a priest as dedication to God (the KJV, which supplies no noun either, reads "he gave him tithes of all" and so is ambiguous in the same way). Radak preserves his father's reading: that Melchizedek gave Abram the tenth, which fits Abram's later refusal of the king of Sodom. Ramban, on the plain reading, sees Abram setting aside the holy part for the priest so that he need take nothing for himself. The "tenth" is the first tithe in the Bible and precedes any Mosaic law; a tenth of the war spoils was a standard royal and temple tax in the ancient Near East.

KJV "tithes" is a plural where Hebrew has a singular "a tenth".

philological_notes.note: 'He delivered, handed over', a verb used in Hosea 11:8 and Proverbs 4:9. Not the same as the noun magen 'shield'. Ibn Ezra: equivalent to 'gave'.
'A tenth': first tithe in the Bible. The subject of the giving is ambiguous.

verses.translation_literal: And the king of Sodom said to Abram: Give me the person[s], and the property take for yourself.
verses.translation_dramatic: And now the king of Sodom spoke, brisk and sure of his terms. "Give me the people. The goods are yours. Take them."
verses.directors_commentary:
The king of Sodom speaks only now, and he opens with a command: "Give me the persons". The Hebrew is blunt, two imperatives (ten, kach) around one contrast: people to me, property to you. This is the law of war in a nutshell: the one who recaptures spoil may keep it, but the owner has a claim on his own people. The king is offering a generous deal, and he is also placing himself above Abram, reasserting his role as the one who disposes of the captives.

The KJV "persons" for nefesh is correct but cold; nefesh is the living person, the soul, the body that breathes, here a word that treats people as property that can be counted. BBE's "prisoners" is an interpretation. Rashi: he asks for only the bodies from the captives Abram has rescued. Radak, noting his father's reading, says that Melchizedek has already granted Abram the tithe.

The pairing of nefesh and rekhush foreshadows the oath: the king thinks Abram will want to be paid, and Abram will refuse to be seen as a man who profits from Sodom.

philological_notes.note: 'The person(s), the living souls': used here as a collective for the captives. In v.16 they are called 'the people', here they are counted as nefesh.

verses.translation_literal: And Abram said to the king of Sodom: I have raised my hand to YHWH, God Most High, buyer of heaven and earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: But Abram answered the king of Sodom, and his voice was quiet and final. "I have raised my hand to the LORD, God Most High, maker and master of heaven and earth."
verses.directors_commentary:
Abram's answer is an oath, and the oath is a gesture: a raised hand. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all hear it as the language of swearing, as in Deuteronomy 32:40 and Daniel 12:7. The perfect tense is performative: "I raise my hand" as he speaks. The KJV "I have lift up mine hand" is formally right but a modern reader will hear only a past action. BBE's "I have taken an oath" gives the sense. Onkelos reads it differently, as a prayer with open hands, and Ramban offers a third reading: the hand lifted as a dedication, a heave offering (terumah), so that anything taken would be consecrated and forbidden.

The real surprise is in the divine name. Melchizedek said only El Elyon. Abram says "YHWH El Elyon", fusing the God of his own covenant with the priest's title. Ibn Ezra explains that he swears by the name which the priest used to bless him; Radak says Abram added the name to turn the hearers away from other gods. The KJV hides this by printing "the LORD, the most high God", as though both were titles; the Hebrew has the proper name first, then the title. By saying it, Abram turns a foreign priest's blessing into worship of his own God, and gives himself a reason that the king of Sodom cannot answer.

philological_notes.note: 'I have raised my hand': the gesture of an oath. Rashi and Radak: it means 'I raise my hand now', swearing; compare Deuteronomy 32:40 and Daniel 12:7.
Only here is the name YHWH joined to the title El Elyon. Melchizedek had only the title; Abram adds the covenant name.

verses.translation_literal: If from a thread and up to a sandal-strap, and if I take from all that [is] yours; and you will not say, 'I, I have made Abram rich.'
verses.translation_dramatic: Not a thread. Not so much as the cord of a sandal. Nothing of yours, not one thing of all that is yours. I will not have you say, "It was I who made Abram rich."
verses.directors_commentary: This is the second half of a sworn oath, and the Hebrew breaks off in mid-sentence: "If from a thread to a sandal-strap, if I take..." The formula "if" with no result clause is a self-curse left unspoken, and it means "I swear I will not." Sforno states the rule: an "if" in Scripture with no conditional verb after it stands for "that not"; he cites Numbers 14:23, 14:30, 1 Samuel 19:6 ("as the LORD lives, he shall not be put to death") and 2 Kings 5:16. The KJV fills the gap with "That I will not take," which is the right sense but hides the oath's raw shape; the actor should leave it broken. The two extremes, a thread and a sandal-strap, are the smallest objects of the poorest man: Ibn Ezra says the thread is what every garment is sewn from and the strap is the leather that ties the shoe. The sharp point is the last clause, with its emphatic "I, I": Abram refuses to let a king of Sodom claim to have made him wealthy. Rashi's reason is that God promised to enrich him, "I will bless you" (12:2). The king may keep the goods; Abram keeps the oath.

philological_notes.note: In an oath, "if" with no result means "surely not": the unspoken part is the curse on oneself. Sforno lists the pattern and its biblical parallels.
"Sandal-strap": the leather that binds the shoe. The KJV's "shoelatchet" is a fair old English equivalent. Ibn Ezra defines it as the leather tying the shoe.
"I made rich": a causative of the root for wealth, so the king would be the cause of Abram's wealth. Rashi hears the answer in God's promise.

verses.translation_literal: Apart from me, only that which the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me: Aner, Eshcol and Mamre, they, let them take their share.
verses.translation_dramatic: "I ask for nothing. Only what my young men have already eaten, and the share of the men who marched beside me. Aner, Eshcol and Mamre: let them take their portion."
verses.directors_commentary:
Abram refuses for himself and insists for others. The sentence is clipped and a little legal: bil'adai, "apart from me" (Radak notes that the final -i is debated, a plural ending or the 'my' of 'me'); then an exception, "only what the young men have eaten", the food already consumed; then the share of the allies. The KJV's "Save only" is accurate, and its "let them take their portion" captures the jussive. BBE adds "Give me nothing", which supplies the verb the Hebrew leaves out.

Abram draws a careful line between his oath and the rights of his allies. His own men (the "young men", hanne'arim) have eaten, and Ibn Ezra says that only means they had eaten the provisions. The allies Aner, Eshcol and Mamre are "masters of covenant" from v.13, and the booty belongs to them under the custom of the day: a share goes to every man who took part. Rashi adds that even though Aner and his brothers stayed with the baggage, David later adopted the principle that the one who guards the supplies shares equally with the one who fights (1 Sam 30:24). Radak: it is their right by custom and law, and Abram has no authority to waive it.

So the final picture is of a man who is generous with his own but scrupulous with others', and who leaves the king of Sodom with no further claim on him.

philological_notes.note: 'Apart from me, except me'. Radak records a debate about the final yod: plural ending or suffix 'my'. Sforno: 'you may take it, since I hold nothing of it.'
'The young men', here Abram's own trained men (Rashi: my servants; Radak: his household-born). Their share is limited to what they have eaten.

events.title: Five Jordan-plain kings rebel against Chedorlaomer
events.narrative_summary: In the days of four named kings of the east, the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela gather in the Valley of Siddim. They had served Chedorlaomer twelve years and rebel in the thirteenth.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: v4 gives the span: twelve years of service, rebellion in the thirteenth year. The start of the service is not tied to any other chronology anchor, so the revolt is anchored on the end of Abram's settling at Mamre (Gen 13:18), the last event before this chapter, with a guessed offset of 1 year and a wide margin of 2 years. The duration is the 13th year (1 year). REGNAL_YEAR because the text numbers the years.
events.ancient_year_marker: In the thirteenth year they rebelled

events.title: Chedorlaomer and his allies strike the peoples east and south
events.narrative_summary: In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings with him defeat the Rephaim, Zuzim, Emim and Horites, then turn back to Kadesh and strike the Amalekites and the Amorites at Hazazon-tamar.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: v5 'in the fourteenth year' follows the thirteenth of v4 directly, so it starts at the revolt's end. The text gives no duration; a march of about 1,500 km with several battles is estimated at 6 months, margin 3 months. Rashi: the fourteenth year counts from the rebellion. REGNAL_YEAR (numbered year); the length is an estimate and does not raise the tier.

events.title: Four kings defeat five in the Valley of Siddim
events.narrative_summary: The five kings go out and draw up in the Valley of Siddim against the four. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah flee and fall into the bitumen pits, and the survivors flee to the hills.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: v8 follows the campaign that ended at Kadesh in v7, then the invaders advance to the valley; no time word. Anchored on the end of the campaign with a 1-month margin for the march from Hazazon-tamar (Engedi, about 28 km from Siddim). Duration 1 day for the battle. Tier follows the fourteenth year that frames the scene.

events.title: The victors plunder Sodom and Gomorrah and take Lot
events.narrative_summary: The victors take all the goods and food of Sodom and Gomorrah and depart. They also take Lot, Abram's nephew who lived in Sodom, with his possessions.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: vv. 11–12 follow the defeat directly with no time word, so the event starts when the battle ends. Duration 2 days for the gathering of spoil and captives, margin 1 day. Tier follows the fourteenth year.

events.title: A fugitive tells Abram that Lot is captured
events.narrative_summary: A survivor comes to Abram the Hebrew, who lives by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, and tells him. Mamre, Eshcol and Aner are Abram's allies.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The fugitive leaves after the capture. Sodom to Mamre is 51 km straight, about 63 km by road; hurry (5 km/h, 50 km a day) gives about 1 day (urim travel). Anchored on the end of the sack. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan names Og and Passover eve; not followed. DAY_SEQUENCE: the scene is counted in days.

events.title: Abram arms 318 men and pursues the captors to Dan
events.narrative_summary: Abram hears that his kinsman has been taken, arms his 318 trained men born in his household and pursues the invaders as far as Dan.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: v14 follows the report directly, so it starts at the end of the report. Mamre to Dan is 195 km straight, about 244 km by road; hurry (5 km/h) gives 48.8 h moving, about 4.5 days (urim travel). The muster is assumed to take a few hours inside this span. Margin 1 day.

events.title: Abram divides his men, strikes by night and pursues to Hobah
events.narrative_summary: Abram and his servants divide against the enemy by night, strike them and chase them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: v15 'by night': Radak reads it as the middle of the night (surprise attack), Rashi and Ramban as after dark; I take the middle watch (22:00) with a 3-hour margin. Starts at the first such time after arrival at Dan (end of the pursuit). Dan to Hobah is 172 km straight; hurry (5 km/h, 50 km a day) gives about 4 days (urim travel, through the Damascus area). Duration 4 days covers attack and pursuit. DIURNAL_HOUR for the night.

events.title: Abram brings back the goods, Lot, the women and the people
events.narrative_summary: Abram recovers all the goods and brings back his kinsman Lot with his possessions, together with the women and the people.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: v16 follows the pursuit; the journey back is implied by the meeting in the Valley of Shaveh in v17. Hobah to Shaveh via Damascus is 335 km straight, about 418 km by road; walking (4 km/h, 28 km a day) with captives gives about 14.5 days (urim travel). The text gives no duration; margin 3 days.

events.title: The king of Sodom goes out to meet Abram
events.narrative_summary: After Abram's return from defeating Chedorlaomer and his allies, the king of Sodom goes out to meet him in the Valley of Shaveh, the King's Valley.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: v17 'after his return' puts the meeting at the end of the return journey. Duration 30 minutes for the meeting; margin 1 day for the arrival.

events.title: Melchizedek brings bread and wine and blesses Abram
events.narrative_summary: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings out bread and wine. He blesses Abram and praises God who delivered his enemies, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: vv. 18–20 give the scene without a time word; it follows the arrival of the king of Sodom (v17) and precedes his speech (v21). Duration about 1 hour for the meal, blessing and the giving of the tithe.

events.title: Abram refuses the king of Sodom's offer of the goods
events.narrative_summary: The king of Sodom asks Abram for the people and offers him the goods. Abram swears by the LORD, God Most High, that he will take nothing, so that the king of Sodom cannot say he made Abram rich. He claims only what the young men ate and the share of Aner, Eshcol and Mamre.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: vv. 21–24 continue the same meeting directly, so the event starts at the end of the blessing. A short exchange of about 30 minutes.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: The defeat of the five kings leaves Sodom and Gomorrah open, and the victors take their goods, food and Lot (14:10–12).
Having struck the peoples as far as Kadesh and Hazazon-tamar, the invaders reach the rebels' valley, where the five kings go out to meet them (14:7–8).
Abram arms his men and pursues because he hears that his kinsman has been taken captive (14:14).
Chedorlaomer comes in the fourteenth year to answer the rebellion of the thirteenth (14:4–5; Rashi: 'for their rebellion').
The night victory and pursuit let Abram recover all the goods, Lot, the women and the people (14:15–16).
The king of Sodom goes out to meet Abram after his return from the victory, with his people restored (14:16–17).
A survivor of the sack carries the news of Lot's capture to Abram (14:12–13).

entities.summary_bio: A people of Canaan. Some of them live at Hazezon-tamar and are struck by Chedorlaomer, while Mamre, Eshcol and Aner are Amorites who ally with Abram.
The people of Sodom taken captive with Lot. Abram brings them back.
An ancient people struck by Chedorlaomer at Shaveh-kiriathaim.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew goyim, 'nations'; whether a place name or 'nations' is uncertain.
entities.summary_bio: The realm of King Tidal, joined to Chedorlaomer's coalition.
The people of the hill country of Seir, struck by Chedorlaomer as far as El-paran.

entities.canonical_name: The five kings of the plain
aliases: kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela
entities.etymology_meaning: A collective label; the text counts them as 'the five'.
entities.summary_bio: The kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela. They served Chedorlaomer twelve years, rebelled in the thirteenth, and are defeated at Siddim.

entities.etymology_meaning: Uncertain; often 'shades' or 'the dead', later used of a tall ancient people.
entities.summary_bio: An ancient people of tall reputation, defeated by Chedorlaomer at Ashteroth-karnaim.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'trained ones, born of his house'; the word chanikh occurs only here.
entities.summary_bio: Three hundred and eighteen trained men born in Abram's household. They follow him in the pursuit and the night attack.

entities.etymology_meaning: Uncertain; sometimes linked to the Zamzummim of Deuteronomy 2.
entities.summary_bio: An ancient people struck by Chedorlaomer at Ham.
One of the five cities of the plain, whose king Shinab rebels.
The territory ('field') of the Amalekites, struck by Chedorlaomer.

entities.etymology_meaning: 'Ashtaroth of the two horns', after the goddess Astarte.
entities.summary_bio: City in Bashan where Chedorlaomer defeats the Rephaim.

entities.etymology_meaning: Babel is explained in Genesis 11 as 'confusion' (a folk etymology); the Akkadian name Bab-ilim means 'gate of God'.
entities.summary_bio: Ancient Mesopotamian city and the land around it. In Genesis 14:1 Amraphel is king of Shinar, the land of Babylon (the registry's mapping).
City of Syria, used to place Hobah.
Northern town to which Abram pursues the captors.
Place on the edge of the wilderness, the limit of Chedorlaomer's strike on the Horites.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably an Elamite name; the Hebrew form resembles 'hidden' or 'eternity'.
entities.summary_bio: Kingdom east of Mesopotamia, ruled by Chedorlaomer.
Mesopotamian kingdom of Arioch.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hazezon-tamar probably 'pruning of the palm'; Engedi is 'spring of the kid'.
entities.summary_bio: Oasis on the Dead Sea (later Engedi, 2 Chr 20:2), home of Amorites struck by Chedorlaomer.
Place where Chedorlaomer strikes the Zuzim.
Place north ('left') of Damascus, the end of Abram's pursuit.
City of Melchizedek, usually identified with later Jerusalem (Ps 76:2).
Oasis, called En-mishpat in this text, where Chedorlaomer turns back and strikes the Amalekites' country.
Valley identified in verse 17 with the Valley of Shaveh, where Abram is met on his return.
Place east of the Jordan named with Shaveh as where the Emim are struck.
The Dead Sea; the text says the Valley of Siddim is, or lies by, the Salt Sea.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'hairy' or 'shaggy', probably of its wooded hills.
entities.summary_bio: Hill country south of the Dead Sea, home of the Horites.
Place (Shaveh-kiriathaim) where the Emim are struck by Chedorlaomer.
Valley full of bitumen pits near the Salt Sea. The five kings muster here and are defeated.
One of the five cities of the plain, whose king Shemeber rebels.

entities.etymology_meaning: Meaning uncertain; sometimes linked to an Akkadian or Amorite name.
entities.summary_bio: King of Shinar and one of the four kings who campaign under Chedorlaomer. He fights the five kings at Siddim and shares in the plunder of Sodom.
An Amorite brother of Mamre and Eshcol, Abram's ally who marches with him against the captors.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably a Hurrian-type name; sometimes compared with Arriwuk.
entities.summary_bio: King of Ellasar and an ally of Chedorlaomer. He takes part in the campaign against the Jordan-plain kings.

entities.etymology_meaning: Meaning uncertain; perhaps 'in evil' (a pun) or a proper name.
entities.summary_bio: King of Sodom, who rebels against Chedorlaomer and fights at Siddim. The king of Sodom who later meets Abram is probably he or his successor.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'in wickedness' (a pun), or a proper name of uncertain sense.
entities.summary_bio: King of Gomorrah, one of the five who rebel. He fights at Siddim.
King of Elam and overlord of the Jordan-plain kings, who served him twelve years. He leads the coalition that crushes the revolt, sacks Sodom and takes Lot captive, until Abram strikes him by night.
An Amorite brother of Mamre and Aner, Abram's ally who marches with him against the captors.
An unnamed survivor of the defeat at Siddim or of the sack of Sodom. He brings Abram the news that Lot is captured.

entities.etymology_meaning: Unnamed; Bela is the older name of Zoar, as the text itself says.
entities.summary_bio: The unnamed fifth king of the plain, ruling Bela (Zoar). He rebels with the others and fights at Siddim.
An Amorite, brother of Eshcol and Aner, in whose oaks Abram lives. He is Abram's covenant ally and later takes his share of the spoil.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'my king is righteous' (or 'Zedek is my king').
entities.summary_bio: King of Salem and priest of God Most High, who brings out bread and wine, blesses Abram and receives a tenth of everything from him. He appears only here in Genesis.

entities.etymology_meaning: Possibly 'name of soaring', or 'soaring on high'; uncertain.
entities.summary_bio: King of Zeboiim, one of the five rebel kings of the plain.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'Sin (the moon-god) is father', or a pun on 'father's tooth'.
entities.summary_bio: King of Admah, one of the five rebel kings of the plain.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably related to the Hittite royal name Tudhaliya.
entities.summary_bio: King of Goiim, an ally of Chedorlaomer. He fights at Siddim and shares in the spoil.

systems.name: Covenant alliance
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Allies were bound by a treaty (berit) and fought together; its partners were called 'masters of the covenant'.
rules_and_mechanics: Allies join in the defence of a partner.

systems.name: Military campaign and battle
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Coalitions of kings campaigned long distances to punish rebels and secure trade routes, then met the enemy in battle array.
rules_and_mechanics: Allied kings march under a lead king.
Territories on the route are struck.
The enemy forms battle lines in a chosen valley.

systems.name: Plunder and taking of captives
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Victors took goods, provisions and people from defeated cities as spoil.
rules_and_mechanics: Movable goods and food are carried off.
The spoil belongs to the victors.

systems.name: Priestly blessing
systems.ancient_near_east_context: A priest-king could bless a victor in the name of his god and provide a meal.
rules_and_mechanics: The priest blesses the person in the name of the god.
The god is praised for the victory.
Bread and wine are brought out.

systems.name: Surprise night attack
systems.ancient_near_east_context: A small force could defeat a larger, tired army by dividing and striking at night.
rules_and_mechanics: The force is divided against the enemy.

systems.name: Tithe
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Giving a tenth of goods to a priest or temple was a recognised offering in the ancient Near East.
rules_and_mechanics: It is given to a priest of the deity.

systems.name: Vassal service to an overlord
systems.ancient_near_east_context: A stronger king imposed tribute on smaller states for years; refusal was rebellion and brought a punitive campaign.
rules_and_mechanics: Subject kings pay tribute and serve the overlord.
The overlord answers with a military expedition.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram, living at the oaks of Mamre, is allied by covenant with Mamre, Eshcol and Aner.
system_instances.significance_note: It supplies allies for the rescue and explains the share they take in verse 24.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Four kings defeat five in the Valley of Siddim; the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fall, the rest flee to the hills.
system_instances.significance_note: The defeat leaves Sodom and Lot exposed.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Chedorlaomer's coalition strikes the Rephaim, Zuzim, Emim, Horites, Amalekites and Amorites.
system_instances.significance_note: It shows the coalition's reach before it turns on the five kings.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Melchizedek brings bread and wine, blesses Abram by God Most High and praises God for the victory.
system_instances.significance_note: It credits the victory to God and introduces a priest-king of Salem.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram divides his force, strikes by night and pursues the enemy to Hobah.
system_instances.significance_note: A small household force defeats a victorious coalition.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram swears by the LORD, God Most High, that he will take nothing of the king of Sodom's, from a thread to a sandal strap.
system_instances.significance_note: It keeps Abram from owing his wealth to Sodom's king; only the young men's food and his allies' shares are excepted.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The victors take the goods and food of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot with his goods.
system_instances.significance_note: Lot's capture draws Abram into the war.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram gives Melchizedek a tenth of everything.
system_instances.significance_note: Abram recognises Melchizedek's priesthood and God Most High.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The plain kings serve Chedorlaomer twelve years, then rebel in the thirteenth.
system_instances.significance_note: The rebellion sets off the whole war of the chapter.

edges.description: Abram arms his 318 men and pursues the captors as far as Dan.
Abram refuses to take anything of the king's, lest the king say he made Abram rich.
Abram brings back Lot, his goods, and the women and people.
Abram divides his force, attacks by night and routs the captors.
Abram lifts his hand to the LORD, God Most High, maker of heaven and earth.
Abram gives Melchizedek a tenth of everything.
The four kings defeat the five kings at Siddim.
The victors take all the goods and food of Sodom.
Chedorlaomer and his allies strike the Amorites of Hazezon-tamar.
Chedorlaomer and his allies strike the Emim at Shaveh-kiriathaim.
Chedorlaomer and his allies strike the Horites in the hill country of Seir.
Chedorlaomer and his allies strike the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim.
Chedorlaomer and his allies strike the Zuzim at Ham.
They take Lot and his goods away.
The fugitive tells Abram the Hebrew what has happened.
Melchizedek says God Most High delivered Abram's enemies into his hand.
Melchizedek blesses Abram by God Most High.
The five kings stop serving Chedorlaomer in the thirteenth year.
The king of Sodom meets Abram on his return from the victory.
The king of Sodom asks for the people and offers Abram the goods.
